canonicalCards.recommendedFirstExperiment: First lower vocal slightly. If that reveals acoustic guitar, restore the fader and test a small broad cut on vocal in the overlap while preserving vocal intelligibility.
stopOrUndo: Stop when both roles are legible; do not force complete spectral separation.

canonicalCards.rationale: Masking is relational. A soloed spectrum cannot determine which source should move or whether the conflict is primarily level, arrangement, or frequency.
canonicalCards.recommendedFirstExperiment: First lower vocal slightly. If that reveals strings, restore the fader and test a small broad cut on vocal in the overlap while preserving vocal emotion.
stopOrUndo: Stop when both roles are legible; do not force complete spectral separation.
Restore the competing-source fader and bypass the diagnostic bands.
canonicalCards.teachingPrinciple: Solve masking with the cheapest relationship change first: level, arrangement, then frequency.
canonicalCards.title: Unmasking strings and vocal
tradeoffs: Complementary EQ can become formulaic and hollow.
A static cut may be unnecessary when the overlap is intermittent.

canonicalCards.recommendedFirstExperiment: Loop the worst notes/hits and test a gentle shelf, filter, or dynamic reduction only where the boom occurs.
stopOrUndo: Back off as soon as the named problem improves but the intended body, attack, clarity, or emotion begins to weaken.
Bypass/delete the diagnostic band and restore the saved plug-in output level.
canonicalCards.teachingPrinciple: A tone word is a clue; use one reversible, context-aware test to identify the relationship causing it.
canonicalCards.title: Diagnosing a boomy full mix
tradeoffs: Excess filtering removes authority and changes the source identity.
A louder or visually smoother curve may create false confidence.

canonicalCards.recommendedFirstExperiment: Use region gain on one obvious outlier in the backing-vocal stack, then replay through the same processing and decide whether the remaining variation needs compression or automation.
stopOrUndo: Stop when the role stays readable and remaining variation feels intentional.
Reset the edited region gain to 0 dB or remove the new automation points.
canonicalCards.teachingPrinciple: Match the control to the timescale: region gain for outliers, compression for short dynamics, automation for musical phrases.
canonicalCards.title: Leveling an inconsistent backing-vocal stack
tradeoffs: Over-leveling removes expression.
Compression can change tone and transient shape.
Automation can become over-detailed and brittle.

canonicalCards.recommendedFirstExperiment: Raise the lead vocal by 1–2 dB for one pass, then restore it and instead lower the most likely competing source by the same small amount; compare which move improves clarity with fewer side effects.
stopOrUndo: Stop when the source reads in context at a natural level; do not force every detail to be equally prominent.
Restore both noted fader positions.
canonicalCards.teachingPrinciple: When a source is audible solo but lost in context, test the relationship before reshaping the source.
canonicalCards.title: When the lead vocal is buried
tradeoffs: Continuous boosting can consume headroom and make the mix harsh or crowded.
Cutting a competing source may weaken its role.

canonicalCards.question: Why does my lead vocal dominate the mix even when its fader does not look very high?
canonicalCards.rationale: Perceived prominence of the lead vocal can come from level, spectrum, dynamics, width, or arrangement. The fader position alone reveals none of those.
canonicalCards.recommendedFirstExperiment: Lower the lead vocal by a small audible amount in the densest section, then return it to the original position and compare at the same monitor level.
stopOrUndo: Stop when the lead vocal supports the song without pulling attention away from the intended focal point.
Return the fader to the noted value or use Undo.
canonicalCards.teachingPrinciple: Perceived loudness is shaped by spectrum, dynamics, and role—not just fader position.

canonicalCards.question: How do I keep the lead vocal in place when some moments are too loud and others disappear?
canonicalCards.rationale: An inconsistent lead vocal may need pre-processing clip/region gain, compression for microdynamics, fader automation for musical rides, or arrangement changes. Each solves a different timescale.
canonicalCards.recommendedFirstExperiment: Use region gain on one obvious outlier in the lead vocal, then replay through the same processing and decide whether the remaining variation needs compression or automation.
stopOrUndo: Stop when the role stays readable and remaining variation feels intentional.
Reset the edited region gain to 0 dB or remove the new automation points.
canonicalCards.teachingPrinciple: Match the control to the timescale: region gain for outliers, compression for short dynamics, automation for musical phrases.
canonicalCards.title: Leveling an inconsistent lead vocal
tradeoffs: Over-leveling removes expression.
Compression can change tone and transient shape.
Automation can become over-detailed and brittle.
